title: Sharpen a kitchen knife on a whetstone at 15 to 20 degrees, both sides, then lay it down edge away
instruction: Sharpen the knife on the whetstone, then put it back on the chopping block.
context: Sharpening a kitchen knife is a familiar household chore: a dull knife slips and needs more force, and many home cooks keep a whetstone for it, as do cooks and butchers who look after their own knives. The trained skill is the angle: the blade is held 15 to 20 degrees off the stone and drawn across it edge first, a few strokes on each face, then the knife is laid down flat with its edge away from the body. Held too steep, the stone grinds a steeper, more obtuse edge that cuts less keenly; held too flat, it grinds the face behind the bevel and scratches the blade without touching the edge; sharpening one face only pushes the edge over into a wire instead of making it sharp.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0; headings are measured from +x towards +y. Chopping block: an end-grain maple butcher block, 12 x 22 x 8 cm, fixed, its center at (16.4, 8.5), its long side at heading 105 degrees (turned 15 degrees from the y axis), its top at z 8. Knife: a 165 mm santoku (Japanese kitchen knife), 100 g, steel blade 16.5 cm long, 4.5 cm tall at the heel and 2 mm thick, its spine running straight for 7 cm and then curving down to the tip, its edge straight with a 6 mm rise over the last 3 cm to the tip, and a bright 6 mm ground bevel along the edge, an octagonal magnolia handle 9.5 cm long and 1.8 to 2.0 cm across with a dark horn ferrule; its balance point 2 cm in front of the bolster. It lies flat on the block, face A down, edge facing away from the robot (heading 15 degrees), the tip pointing left along the block, the bolster at (18.4, 0.8) and the front 3 cm of the handle on the block, the rest of the handle reaching past the block's right-hand edge towards (20.9, -8.4) so a hand can close round it. Whetstone: an orange 1000-grit combination stone, 18 x 6 x 2.5 cm, in a black rubber non-slip holder (21 x 8 x 1.5 cm with end clamps 3 cm tall) on a 6 cm wooden sharpening stand, all fixed, centered at (39.4, -5.5), its long side at heading -15 degrees (pointing away from the robot and slightly right), the stone's top at z 10. The left arm is not needed; both arms start at their home pose.
scoring: The scorer reads the knife's pose and both grippers every control step (20 Hz). Sharpening angle: measured across the blade, the angle its width (spine to edge) tilts below the stone's level top, edge down; a knife pitched tip-down about its width is not at an angle. Level: the blade's length (handle to tip) within 5 degrees of horizontal, since a whetstone stroke keeps the edge lying along the stone and a 5 degree pitch already lifts the far end of a 6 cm contact 5 mm off it; the edge's rise near the tip comes onto the stone with the handle lifted about 3 degrees, as a sharpener does for the tip, inside this limit. On the stone: the knife held (both fingers of a gripper touching the handle, their opening stopped by its 1.8 to 2.0 cm girth, so a knife pushed by a hand merely near it does not count), the edge lower than the spine, and touching: its lowest point over the stone within 0.5 mm of the stone's top (the knife's collider rests on the stone's, so a held-up knife does not count). The scorer checks 16 points about 1 cm apart along the edge, from 0.5 cm past the heel to 16.2 cm, 3 mm short of the point, where the edge curves up to meet the spine; a point within 1 mm of the stone's top is on it. A stroke: one touch on the stone (lifting off ends it) in which the knife moves at least 5 cm in the direction its edge faces (edge leading) while the sharpening angle is 13 to 22 degrees (the 15 to 20 degree range for kitchen knives, plus 2 degrees each way for a hand-held angle), the blade is level and at least 3 points (about 3 cm, half the stone's 6 cm width) are on the stone, so dragging only the tip or heel does not count. Edge-trailing travel, or flatter than 13 degrees (grinding the face behind the bevel), does not count. Strokes are counted per face (which face is down). An edge point is worked on a face once it has been on the stone for 5 cm of such travel. The stone is 6 cm across and the edge 16.5 cm long, so working most of the edge means moving the knife along so the heel, middle and tip each cross the stone. A touch with 2 cm of travel steeper than 22 degrees (it works a steeper, more obtuse micro-bevel, not the 15 to 20 degree edge), or whose edge drops 3 mm below the stone's top just past an end within 0.5 s of leaving it (rolled off the end instead of lifted), counts toward neither strokes nor worked edge; the trial is not zeroed. Put down safely: let go (no part of either gripper touching the knife; a gap of 2 mm or less between the knife and the gripper's own shape counts as touching), lying on the block (its blade over the block, the edge within 1 cm of its top, faces within 20 degrees of level), and the edge facing away from the robot (within 60 degrees of +x), so a knife is not left in the hand or on the stone and the next hand that reaches for the handle does not meet the edge. Score: 0 with fewer than 3 strokes on both faces, including doing nothing; 0.25 with 3 or more on one face only (the edge is pushed over into a wire, not sharp); 0.5 with 3 or more on each face but fewer than 12 of the 16 edge points (three quarters of the edge) worked on a face (the right technique, but a quarter or more of the edge still dull); 0.75 with 3 or more strokes and 12 points worked on each face (sharpened, but the knife not put down safely); 1.0 for that and the knife put down safely, held for 1 s. Where the arms end is not scored. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1. A real trial: color both edge bevels with a marker beforehand and read the angle on the side video against 15, 20 and 22 degree cards, watching for roll-offs. A correct angle removes the ink right at the edge only, and it must be gone along at least three quarters of the edge on each face (measure the inked stretches with a ruler); a knife held off the stone removes no ink. The put-down is checked on the top photo with a protractor.
reset_notes: Put the knife back flat on the block, face A down, edge away, at the start position (bolster at (18.4, 0.8)); the stone, holder, stand and block are fixed. For a real trial use a dulled knife and re-ink the bevel; soak the stone 10 minutes beforehand.
fidelity: Nothing is ground: sharpness is scored from the knife's pose while it is on the stone, not from material removed; a real trial checks the marker ink on the bevels instead. The stone is dry and rigid with no slurry. The knife is 100 g (a real one is about 140 g) and is gripped by a single box collider handle; turned boxes make the blade's collider follow the tip's rise. The stone stand is taller than usual (6 cm) so the arm's wrist clears the bench, and strokes are scored at full size.
